title: The Yodeling Flute Fiasco
markdown:
In the frosty blue heart of the Sky-Kissed Mountains, where winding roads twisted like sleepy snakes and hot springs puffed mist into the air, lived wizard Caspar. His home was ice and snow, with the distant clang of hammers from markets built under stone arches. Caspar was a wizard of strict routines and stylish robes. He liked to appear calm and in control. His constant friend, a sleek black cat named Moth, had eyes like dark glass that saw everything. Moth wasn’t just a pet; he was a furry purring encyclopedia of old stories, a silent judge, and, when needed, a surprisingly quick helper.

The messenger arrived in a swirl of snow, gasping, so pale he looked dipped in frosty water, and Caspar’s perfect composure flickered for just a second.

“Wizard Caspar. Lady Elara has arrived. But the north pass is blocked by a massive snowdrift. A real mountain of white.”

“Massive,” Caspar whispered, tasting the word like a sour grape. He straightened a perfectly placed cuff. Moth, his sleek black cat, eyes like dark glass, blinked. “Do not worry, Moth. A small detour is a chance for a more interesting route. Precision means finding the right way, even if it has a few more surprises.”

Crisis one: the guest, the blocked pass, the image of flawless hosting already cracking like an icicle. Caspar liked routines and stylish robes. He liked to appear calm. Moth was a furry encyclopedia of old stories, a silent judge, and, when needed, a quick helper.

Their trek began, a careful dance of Caspar’s measured steps and Moth’s silent flowing moves. The air nipped at their faces, and the wind hummed tales of winter’s power, a constant roar of swirling snow. They headed down towards the busy market town of Frostfall, where carved arches offered a brief chilly break from the sharp winds. Here they needed supplies: dried berries packed with sweet flavour, warm spiced nuts that popped with taste, and a sturdy flask of invisibility potion, for those unexpected, or perhaps just awkward, meetings. Lady Elara, somewhere behind them in the care of the pale messenger, would expect a host who had never heard of a blocked pass. Caspar intended to be that host, even if he had to invent him on the way.

Crisis two, worse: Grumblebelly’s stall, a messy cave of questionable goods and more questionable smells.

“Ah, Wizard Caspar,” cackled the goblin, teeth stained with something ancient and sticky, a finger with too many joints. “Here to check out my best items? Just the thing for your mountain climb. A wonder of musical invention, guaranteed to cheer anyone.” Dust flying. Not the climbing ropes Caspar had listed in his mind. A brightly coloured, fancy, utterly useless yodeling flute. “For making a long climb more fun.” Grin wider than a hungry troll’s mouth.

Caspar’s calm nearly shattered. “A yodeling flute.” Voice dangerously smooth. “While I appreciate your enthusiastic ideas, we need useful gear. Strong tools. Not toys. This is pointless.”

Moth, on a wobbly pile of boxes, let out a soft mrrrow that in cat meant: this is going to be good.

Reflection: Caspar tasted sour grape again, decided he would not panic in front of a goblin, and looked for a better tool than dignity.

Crisis three, worst: a vast shadow over the market. Ignis Flutterwing, scales like a thousand jewels, incredibly powerful, mostly concerned with looking elegant, as if fire were an impolite habit. “Hmph.” Far-off thunder. “One hopes my arrival doesn’t cause too much fuss. I’m just passing through, looking for a quiet spot to think about cloud shapes. I really dislike being the centre of attention.”

Caspar saw a spark. “Ah, noble Ignis Flutterwing. Perfect timing. We’ve encountered a small problem. This item,” extreme distaste at the flute, “is no help for climbing, ropes, or any practical reason. We need something to tie ropes to. Something that can handle the harshest winds. Perhaps a dragon’s claw could make a most excellent anchor.”

Ignis puffed. Surprise, then annoyance. “A dragon’s claw? For tying ropes? That’s not proper behaviour. You don’t just ask for a dragon’s body part for knot-tying. Undignified. Messy. My claws are for polishing treasure, or carefully scraping sea creatures off my wings.” Pride, inconvenient, was touched. “However,” looking at the flute with utter disgust, “that instrument is an offence to good taste and would disturb the mountain’s peace. If I must help, it will be to get rid of that disaster.”

A quick, almost delicate nudge of the nose. The flute tumbled, thump, into a deep snowdrift, buried, silenced by the mountain’s white blanket.

“There. Problem solved. A small act of public service. Now, if you’ll excuse me, the Northern Lights are about to start, and one wouldn’t want to miss such a sky performance.”

Climax: Caspar seized the opening. Real strong rope, the kind that would not break with a determined mountain goat on it. A knowing look at Moth. He guided Lady Elara with a smoothness that hid the near-disaster. Moth, a quick flick of paw, nudged a perfectly sized enchanted pebble from his own secret collection toward Caspar’s boot. Anchor points stayed firm against gusts and naughty mountain spirits.

Lady Elara left shining with admiration, praising remarkably smooth and clever guiding. Caspar had not really panicked, not in front of the guest. He had adjusted. Improvised. Kept the image, with help from a dragon who hated bad music and a cat who found lost magic.

Later, in the tower, wind like a lonely wolf, Caspar poured spiced cider. Moth curled on his lap, a happy furry engine.

“A successful trip, wouldn’t you say, Moth? The goblin’s habit of misplaced items was a wrinkle. We handled it.”

Moth stretched, settled deeper, firelight in dark glass eyes. He did not explain that he was home. The cider steamed. Somewhere under a snowdrift, a yodeling flute remained quiet, which was the kindest thing the mountain had done all day.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
